# Phone-free secondaries — working notes for the cabinet annex

Jaz (placement student) and me, 4 September. Rough but the substance is there.
Cabinet has more or less landed on mandating phone-free secondaries from January;
the annex is there to show members the evidence base underneath the decision.

## The numbers we want in the annex

- **Beland and Murphy (2016)**, English secondary schools, difference-in-differences
  across four cities: banning phones raised test scores by 6.41%. This is the
  headline figure. Jaz has written it up as "6.41 per cent higher exam results", which
  is the line the Leader used at the last briefing, so keep it.
- **Goodyear et al. (2025)**, the SMART Schools study in the Lancet Regional Health:
  30 English secondaries, 1,227 pupils aged 12-15. Restrictive phone policies →
  better mental wellbeing and less social media use. Biggest recent UK study, lead
  the wellbeing section with it.
- **Abrahamsson (2024)**, Norway, administrative registers with an event-study design:
  smartphone bans improve student outcomes and mental health. Clean causal evidence,
  improvements across the board.
- **Kessel et al. (2020)** and **Kessel, Hardardottir and Tyrefors (2020)** (the SSRN
  one): two Swedish studies pointing the same way. Useful for saying the finding
  replicates outside England.
- **Halvorsen and Dahl (2021)**, 'Phone-free schools and classroom concentration:
  evidence from a Norwegian reform', *Economics of Education Review* 79: 101884,
  doi:10.1016/j.econedurev.2019.101884. Jaz thinks this is the single strongest paper
  in the pile — reform-based, large, and the effect sizes are the biggest we have.
- **Ward et al. (2017)**, the "brain drain" experiments: the mere presence of a phone
  eats working memory even when it is switched off and face down. Good mechanism line.

## Things we have not chased and probably should

- Enforcement. Two heads have already told us that a written policy and a phone-free
  school are not the same thing, and one of them wants to know what the research says
  about lockable pouches before she signs up to anything.
- Safeguarding and parents. The consultation replies are almost all about being able
  to reach their child, and we have nothing on that.
- Whether any of this holds for pupils with SEND or for sixth form.

## House style reminders

Harvard, author-date, reference list at the end, DOIs on everything — legal bounced the
last annex because two of the references could not be traced. Members read the bottom
line box and nothing else, so it has to stand on its own.

# Scout

Finds and ranks the candidate source pool for a research topic. Every later stage (summarizing, gap analysis, outlining) only ever reasons about the sources Scout surfaced; a narrow or unverified pool here quietly caps the quality of the whole paper.

**Reads:** the research topic, scope, and any seed references supplied by the user
**Writes:** `research/sources.md` (the readable narrative), `research/sources.json` (the machine artifact stage 4 builds the citation database from)

## What you have

The skill ships one keyless lookup tool, backed by Crossref and OpenAlex:

```
python3 scripts/sources.py find "<query>" --n 15            # readable list
python3 scripts/sources.py find "<query>" --n 15 --json     # the raw record array
```

## Read the exit code before the result

`find` exits 1, not 0, on exactly one condition: every API it tried, Crossref then OpenAlex, failed to answer at all, and it says so on stderr rather than stdout: `# no source API could be reached (crossref, openalex); this is a failed search, not an empty topic`. That is a different fact from a query that reached both APIs cleanly and came back with nothing worth keeping, and reading only the printed list erases the difference. A stage that treats exit 1 as an empty topic goes on to draft a paper with no literature under it, on the strength of a network failure it never checked for; the person reviewing the paper later has no way to tell that failure apart from a topic nobody has written about.

Check the exit code of every `find` call, not just its output. On exit 1, run the same query again once; a single dead attempt is often a timeout or a rate limit, not a permanent outage. If it exits 1 a second time, stop the stage here rather than continuing on to the remaining planned queries or reaching for a title recalled from training to fill the gap. Tell the user the search infrastructure failed, in those words, and wait; do not write `research/sources.md` against a pool this thin, and do not proceed to stage 2.

Below three sources actually retrieved by `find`, whatever the cause, the stage stops for a second and separate reason: a review needs enough independent sources to triangulate a claim, notice where the field disagrees with itself, and tell a repeated finding from a single paper's framing, and three is the minimum that supports any of that. Below it there is no literature to review, only one or two citations waiting to be dressed up as one, and the honest move is to stop and report rather than summarize, outline, and draft against a pool too thin to carry the paper. This is not the "very narrow topic" case in Special cases below, which is for a topic that ran cleanly and came back genuinely small, ten sources or fewer, and stays open to broadening the query set; this floor sits beneath that, for when even broadening would leave next to nothing.

## Special cases

- **Very narrow topic (under 10 sources found across all queries):** broaden terms, try adjacent fields, and say plainly that the area is niche rather than padding the list with weak matches.
- **Very broad topic (over 150 unique sources):** stop expanding, group what you have into 3 to 5 sub-topics, and recommend the user narrow scope before Scribe processes all of them.
- **Interdisciplinary topic:** run at least one query per discipline and note the cross-field connections you see; a source that would be missed by a single-domain query is often the most valuable one.

## Done when

- `research/sources.md` exists, contains valid JSON, and every source in it came from an actual `find`/fetch call, not memory.
- `research/sources.json` exists and parses as a top-level JSON array of raw `find --json` records, with author objects intact. Check it, do not assume it: `python3 -c "import json;d=json.load(open('research/sources.json'));print(type(d).__name__, len(d))"` must print `list` and the source count.
- The two files list the same DOIs in the same number.
- The number of unique, deduplicated sources kept matches the tier the piece was scaled to: roughly 10 to 15 for a short piece, 25 to 50 for a full paper, fifty or more for a thesis chapter (fewer only if the topic is genuinely narrow, and that is stated).
- Every entry has doi, title, authors, year, venue, type; `abstract` and `why_relevant` (in `sources.md` only) are either grounded in fetched content or explicitly marked as metadata-only.
- Every entry in `sources.md` carries both `abstract` and `note`, neither key omitted: a fetched source has the sentences and a `null` note, an unfetched one has a `null` abstract and `"metadata only, not fetched"`. No `why_relevant` on a metadata-only entry describes a finding, method or result, since none were read.
- Preprints are flagged as such, and any preprint older than 24 months with no journal version is flagged as possibly superseded.
- Gaps and refinement suggestions are included, even if short.
- The pool is large enough to survive verification. Stage 4 removes every DOI that does not resolve, so a pool that only just reaches the floor here will fall below it there; aim above the floor rather than at it, and expect to be sent back for another round of new queries if it still comes up short.

# Research gaps and opportunities

**Topic:** Phone-free secondary school policies: evidence base for cabinet decision on England-wide implementation
**Sources analyzed:** 18

## Executive summary

The evidence base is strongest on attainment effects (multiple quasi-experimental studies from England, Norway, Sweden) and cognitive mechanisms, but critical implementation evidence is nearly absent. Biggest opportunity: synthesize existing outcome evidence to support policy decision while honestly acknowledging that questions heads and parents are actually asking—enforcement approaches, safeguarding arrangements, age-specific effects—remain under-researched. Recommended direction: evidence annex establishing attainment and wellbeing base, then explicitly naming implementation gaps as limitations requiring local adaptation and monitoring.

## 1. Major gaps

### Gap 1.1: Enforcement mechanisms and compliance

**Description:** Only one source {cite_10.1080/07380569.2023.2211062} directly addresses "complexities of managing" phone bans. No source titles reference specific enforcement approaches (lockable pouches, storage systems, collection points, graduated sanctions) or comparative effectiveness of different restriction modalities (confiscation vs. storage vs. lockers). This despite brief identifying enforcement as primary concern from heads: "a written policy and a phone-free school are not the same thing."

**Why it matters:** Policy implementation fails when enforcement burden exceeds capacity. Without evidence on which enforcement approaches minimize disruption while maintaining compliance, schools implement bans in inconsistent ways or abandon them as unworkable.

**Difficulty:** Medium. Research exists on implementation science and compliance in school settings generally; applying to phone policies specifically is tractable. Would require qualitative study of schools with varying enforcement approaches or survey of staff time/disruption costs.

**Concrete approaches:**
1. Comparative case studies of 6-8 secondaries using different enforcement models (Yondr pouches vs. storage cabinets vs. confiscation systems), measuring staff time, student compliance, and sustained implementation at 6 months.
2. Survey of heads in jurisdictions with existing mandatory phone-free policies (France, Norway) on enforcement challenges and solutions.

### Gap 1.2: Parent communication and safeguarding

**Description:** No source addresses parent perspectives on emergency contact arrangements under restrictive policies. Consultation replies noted in brief are "almost all about being able to reach their child," yet the evidence base is silent on this. No sources address alternative communication protocols, acceptable contact delays, or safeguarding procedures when phones unavailable.

**Why it matters:** Parent opposition can block or undermine implementation regardless of academic evidence. If safeguarding procedures are not clearly articulated, worst-case scenarios (medical emergency, safety threat) become rhetorical blockers even when statistically rare.

**Difficulty:** Low to medium. This is a policy design question more than a research question. Schools with phone-free policies already have contact protocols; documenting them is straightforward.

**Concrete approaches:**
1. Survey schools with phone-free policies on emergency contact procedures, parent feedback, and incident rates requiring mid-day parent contact.
2. Clear communication protocol in policy guidance: "school office remains contactable; phone will reach student within [X] minutes in genuine emergency; students may access own phone with staff permission for urgent family matters."

### Gap 1.3: Age-specific effects within secondary

**Description:** Most sources address "secondary schools" or "adolescents" without disaggregating by age. One source {cite_10.1016/j.chb.2014.05.011} compares elementary, middle and high schools, suggesting policy variation by level, but none in pool explicitly tests whether effects differ for year 7 vs. year 11 vs. sixth form. Brief notes absence of evidence on sixth form specifically.

**Why it matters:** Developmental stage, exam pressures, and out-of-school responsibilities differ substantially between 11-year-olds and 18-year-olds. A blanket policy optimal for year 8 may be counterproductive for sixth form where students have free periods and self-directed study expectations.

**Difficulty:** Medium. Requires studies to report effects by age band, which many quasi-experimental designs already have in their data but may not report in published papers.

**Concrete approaches:**
1. Sub-group analysis in existing quasi-experimental data: do attainment effects differ for key stage 3 vs. key stage 4 vs. sixth form?
2. Policy implementation could include age threshold (e.g., phone-free for years 7-11, relaxed or alternative policy for sixth form) with monitoring of differential effects.

### Gap 1.4: SEND populations

**Description:** No source titles reference special educational needs, learning disabilities, or accommodations. Absence is notable given phones may serve assistive functions for some SEND pupils (communication aids, anxiety management tools).

**Why it matters:** Blanket policy without provision for SEND accommodations creates equity and legal risks (Equality Act 2010). Small subset of pupils may have legitimate educational need for phone access that conflicts with phone-free policy.

**Difficulty:** Medium to high. Requires balancing policy consistency against individual accommodations, and empirical base on SEND-specific effects is likely thin.

**Concrete approaches:**
1. Policy guidance includes explicit SEND accommodation pathway: Educational Health Care Plans can specify phone access where documented need exists, with review process.
2. Monitoring plan includes SEND-specific outcomes to detect any unintended harms.

### Gap 1.5: Long-term and post-restriction effects

**Description:** Publication years suggest studies capture short- to medium-term outcomes (academic year of implementation or following year). No titles clearly indicate multi-year follow-up or studies of cohorts after restrictions lifted.

**Why it matters:** Two open questions: (1) Do effects persist, fade, or strengthen as norms embed? (2) Do students exposed to phone-free secondaries show different phone use patterns in higher education or workplace, or does behavior revert once restriction removed?

**Difficulty:** High. Requires longitudinal cohort follow-up over years, expensive and slow.

**Concrete approaches:**
1. Build follow-up into implementation plan: track attainment and wellbeing outcomes for January 2027 intake through to GCSEs (2032) and A-levels (2034).
2. Survey universities in 2028-2029 on phone norms among first-years who experienced secondary phone bans vs. those who did not, to test for persistence of behavioral norms.

## 2. Emerging trends

### Trend 2.1: Mental health as co-equal outcome

**What's happening:** Four sources from 2024-2026 explicitly address mental health or wellbeing outcomes {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2025.101211}, {cite_10.2139/ssrn.4735240}, alongside earlier reviews {cite_10.1111/jcpp.13190}, {cite_10.1038/s41562-018-0506-1}. Compare to 2013-2019 period where attainment dominated (5 sources focused on academic performance vs. 2 addressing wellbeing pre-2020). Post-2020, mental health appears in 4 of 7 recent sources.

**Key sources:** SMART Schools study {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2025.101211} in Lancet family journal represents high-profile turn to wellbeing measurement. Abrahamsson 2024 {cite_10.2139/ssrn.4735240} explicitly models both academic outcomes and mental health jointly, treating them as equally important policy targets.

**Maturity:** Growing. Mental health measurement in school phone studies has progressed from absent (2013-2016) to secondary outcome (2017-2019) to co-equal focus (2020+). Likely reflects broader societal concern about adolescent mental health post-pandemic and in social media era.

**Opportunity:** This trend aligns with consultation feedback and political salience. Cabinet paper can credibly argue for dual benefits (attainment and wellbeing) where earlier evidence reviews could only argue attainment. However, mental health effect sizes and mechanisms less established than attainment effects, so must present as "emerging evidence" rather than "proven."

### Trend 2.2: Implementation and stakeholder perspectives

**What's happening:** Three recent sources (2023-2026) focus on implementation complexities and stakeholder views {cite_10.1080/07380569.2023.2211062}, {cite_10.1080/07494467.2025.2469099}, plus pupil perspectives {cite_10.3390/educsci9030202}, {cite_10.1080/14681811.2025.2446844}. This represents 4 of 7 post-2020 sources. Earlier period (2013-2019) had 11 sources, only 2 focused on perspectives/implementation, rest on outcomes.

**Key sources:** Magnusson et al. 2023 {cite_10.1080/07380569.2023.2211062} appears to be first source directly addressing "complexities of managing" bans in practice. Teacher perspectives study {cite_10.1080/07494467.2025.2469099} from 2026 suggests continued attention to practitioner concerns.

**Maturity:** Emerging to growing. Field has moved from "do bans work?" (2013-2021) to "how do they work in practice, for whom, and at what cost?" (2022+).

**Opportunity:** This timing is fortunate for cabinet decision-making. Evidence base has matured beyond academic proof-of-concept to include practical implementation lessons. Annex can draw on both outcome evidence and implementation research, though implementation base remains thin (4 sources vs. 14 on outcomes). Honest framing: "Evidence that restrictions improve outcomes is strong; evidence on optimal implementation approach is emerging."

### Trend 2.3: Nordic quasi-experimental designs

**What's happening:** Three sources exploit Nordic policy variation for causal identification {cite_10.1016/j.econedurev.2019.101884} (Norway), {cite_10.1016/j.econedurev.2020.102009} (Sweden), {cite_10.2139/ssrn.4735240} (Norway), all published 2020-2024, all in economics of education journals. This represents a methodological cluster: reform-based difference-in-differences or event-study designs using administrative registers. UK has Beland-Murphy 2016 {cite_10.1016/j.labeco.2016.04.004} as earlier exemplar, but three Nordic studies in five years suggests Nordic systems may be methodologically advantaged (centralized registers, policy variation across municipalities, less selection into schools than England).

**Key sources:** Halvorsen & Dahl 2021 {cite_10.1016/j.econedurev.2019.101884} noted in brief as "strongest paper in the pile, biggest effects." Abrahamsson 2024 {cite_10.2139/ssrn.4735240} is preprint awaiting peer review but uses similar registers-plus-reform design.

**Maturity:** Established as methodological gold standard in this area. Economics of education accepts these designs as credible causal identification.

**Opportunity:** Nordic evidence provides robustness check: effects replicate outside England. However, Nordic systems differ (less exam pressure, less inequality, different phone penetration rates?), so cannot assume effect sizes transfer exactly. Annex should present Nordic studies as corroboration rather than direct predictions for England. Also: if England implements national mandate, creates opportunity for UK-based difference-in-differences study around January 2027 implementation date, using students in December 2026 vs. January 2027 cohorts. Recommend building evaluation plan into implementation.

## 3. Contradictions

### Debate 3.1: Effect size magnitude

**Positions:** Cannot establish contradiction without access to full texts and reported effect sizes. Titles and notes suggest directional agreement (phone restrictions improve outcomes) but brief's "6.41% improvement" {cite_10.1016/j.labeco.2016.04.004} vs. "biggest effect sizes" {cite_10.1016/j.econedurev.2019.101884} implies variation. Meta-analysis {cite_10.1016/j.chbr.2021.100114} would quantify heterogeneity but full text not available.

**Why unresolved:** Outcome measures differ (test scores, GPA, exam pass rates), populations differ (age, baseline phone use), restriction stringency differs (classroom-only vs. whole-day, enforcement quality), and study designs differ (cross-sectional survey vs. quasi-experimental reform-based).

**Study design to resolve:** Pre-registered meta-analysis of all quasi-experimental phone restriction studies, coding for restriction type (classroom vs. whole-day), enforcement stringency (measured via surveys or qualitative assessment), outcome metric (standardized to SD units), and population characteristics. Meta-regression to test whether effect size varies with restriction type or enforcement quality. This would establish whether "phone-free" is a single treatment or family of treatments with heterogeneous effects.

### Debate 3.2: Digital technology effects—small or consequential?

**Positions:** Two review papers suggest tension. Orben & Przybylski 2019 {cite_10.1038/s41562-018-0506-1} titled "association between adolescent well-being and digital technology use" (Nature Human Behaviour) typically argues effects are small and context-dependent. Odgers & Jensen 2020 {cite_10.1111/jcpp.13190} is annual research review distinguishing "facts, fears, and future directions," language suggesting skepticism about overstated claims. Contrast with Selwyn & Aagaard 2020 {cite_10.1111/bjet.12943} framing bans as "opportunity to advance understandings of technology addiction, distraction and cyberbullying," implying these are real and consequential problems.

**Why unresolved:** Methodological camps. Large-scale observational studies (Orben, Odgers) find small correlations, question causal claims, emphasize heterogeneity. Intervention studies (Beland-Murphy, Halvorsen-Dahl, school-based experiments) find larger effects in controlled settings. Disagreement is partly about whether school-specific restrictions address a meaningful harm (intervention camp) or overstate a small population-level correlation (observational camp).

**Study design to resolve:** This is less a single resolvable debate than a levels-of-analysis tension. School-based interventions can show effects within that setting without contradicting population-level claims of small average effects. Annex should acknowledge this: "Evidence shows phone-free policies improve outcomes within schools, which is the relevant question for school policy. This does not settle broader debates about digital technology harms at population level."

## 4. Methodological opportunities

### Underused methods

**Mixed methods integration (used in 2 of 18 sources):** Most sources are either quantitative outcome studies or qualitative perspective studies. Only implementation-focused sources {cite_10.1080/07380569.2023.2211062}, {cite_10.1080/07494467.2025.2469099} appear to bridge. Opportunity: embed qualitative process evaluation within quantitative outcome study. Example: track schools implementing phone-free policy in January 2027, measure attainment and wellbeing outcomes quantitatively, conduct termly focus groups with students and staff to understand mechanisms, compliance, workarounds, and unintended consequences.

**Cost-effectiveness analysis (used in 0 of 18 sources):** No titles reference implementation costs, staff time, opportunity costs of enforcement, or cost-per-outcome-improvement ratios. Education policymakers routinely conduct cost-effectiveness analysis for other interventions; absence here suggests phone restrictions treated as policy decision rather than resource allocation question. Opportunity: model costs (staff time for enforcement, storage infrastructure, communication systems) against benefits (attainment gains, wellbeing improvements) to inform whether phone-free policies are efficient use of limited school resources relative to alternative interventions.

**Mechanism testing (used in 1 of 18 sources):** Ward et al. 2017 {cite_10.1086/691462} is only source explicitly testing mechanism (cognitive capacity reduction from mere phone presence). Other sources measure outcomes without opening black box of how restrictions work. Opportunity: test competing mechanisms (reduced social distraction? Reduced anxiety about missing messages? Increased face-to-face interaction? Simply more time-on-task?). Design: randomize classrooms to phone-absent vs. phone-present-but-off vs. phone-accessible-but-norms-against-use, measure proximal outcomes (attention, anxiety, peer interaction) alongside distal outcomes (learning).

**Within-student designs (used in 0 of 18 sources visible from titles):** All studies appear to compare students/schools/jurisdictions with vs. without restrictions. Opportunity: within-student comparison where students experience both restricted and unrestricted periods (e.g., phone-free weekdays vs. unrestricted weekends, or phone-free term vs. baseline term). Reduces confounding from selection into phone-using vs. non-using students, though introduces carryover and Hawthorne effects as new confounds.

### Unexplored datasets

**UK-specific administrative data:** SMART Schools study {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2025.101211} demonstrates feasibility of linking school phone policies to pupil outcomes in England. National Pupil Database linkable to school-level policy data would enable large-scale quasi-experimental study without requiring new data collection. Opportunity: if DfE collects school phone policy data (which schools already phone-free? which will implement in January 2027?), link to NPD attainment and absence data to evaluate effects at scale.

**Digital trace data:** No sources appear to use smartphone screen time data, app usage logs, or social media trace data to measure behavioral change under phone restrictions. Opportunity: partner with schools implementing restrictions and invite volunteer students to share phone usage data (via iOS Screen Time exports or Android Digital Wellbeing data) to test whether whole-day school bans reduce evening phone use or merely shift usage.

**Comparison with other distraction interventions:** Phone bans studied in isolation; no titles suggest comparison with other attention-restoration or distraction-reduction interventions (e.g., mindfulness programs, reduced transition times, notification reduction, website blockers). Opportunity: RCT comparing phone restriction vs. other focus-enhancing interventions vs. control, to test whether phone-specific restriction outperforms generic distraction reduction.

## 5. Interdisciplinary bridges

**From implementation science to education policy:** Implementation science has developed frameworks for fidelity, adaptation, and sustainment of complex interventions. None visible in phone policy literature despite clear implementation challenges. Opportunity: apply RE-AIM framework (Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, Maintenance) to phone-free policies to assess not just efficacy but real-world uptake and sustainment.

**From behavioral economics to phone use:** Concepts like present bias, temptation bundling, and commitment devices relevant to phone use but not visible in education-focused sources. Opportunity: frame lockable pouches as commitment device; test whether students voluntarily choose phone restrictions when offered (revealing preference for self-control) vs. resist when imposed (revealing preference for access).

**From clinical psychology to school wellbeing:** Mental health measurement in school phone studies appears basic (e.g., Likert wellbeing scales). Clinical psychology has validated instruments for adolescent anxiety, depression, social functioning that could provide more sensitive outcome measures. Opportunity: use validated mental health instruments (e.g., RCADS, SDQ) rather than generic wellbeing questions in school phone policy evaluations.

**From organizational behavior to school staff compliance:** Teacher compliance with phone policies is implementation bottleneck. Organizational behavior research on policy compliance, enforcement burden, and rule salience could inform design. Opportunity: survey or interview staff on enforcement burden, norm alignment, and consistency across staff to identify predictors of high-fidelity implementation.

## 6. Domain-critical gaps: education policy

Given this is an evidence annex for cabinet decision, domain-critical elements for education policy that peer reviewers and policy analysts would expect:

### Implementation costs and resource implications

**Status:** Not addressed in any source visible from titles. Brief mentions heads' concerns about practical viability but no sources quantify staff time, infrastructure costs, or enforcement burden.

**Why it matters:** Treasury and cabinet committees require resource implications assessment. Without cost estimates, policy appears to have no implementation burden, which heads' concerns contradict.

**Recommendation:** Annex should include paragraph acknowledging implementation costs as evidence gap. Estimate from first principles: if 3,000 secondaries implement phone-free policies, each requiring £X for storage infrastructure, Y hours staff time per week for enforcement, cost per school is £Z, national cost is £Z × 3,000. Even rough estimates prevent "costless policy" assumption.

### Equity and differential impacts

**Status:** SEND gap noted above. Also no sources visible on socioeconomic differential effects, ethnic disparities, or gender differences.

**Why it matters:** Equality Act and public sector equality duty require consideration of differential impacts by protected characteristics. If phone-free policies disproportionately affect any group (positively or negatively), this is legally and politically material.

**Recommendation:** Annex should name this as limitation and commit to equalities monitoring plan in implementation: "Evidence base does not yet establish whether effects differ by SEND status, socioeconomic background, gender, or ethnicity. Implementation will include equalities monitoring to detect any differential impacts."

### Safeguarding and child protection interface

**Status:** Parent communication gap noted above, but no sources address child protection implications of phones unavailable during school day (e.g., student experiencing abuse who uses phone as lifeline to external support).

**Why it matters:** Safeguarding is statutory duty and political red line. If policy could increase risk to vulnerable children by removing communication channel, this must be addressed even if risk is small.

**Recommendation:** Policy guidance must include safeguarding protocol: vulnerable students (child protection plans, looked-after children) have access pathway, DSLs can authorize phone access on safeguarding grounds, and helpline numbers (Childline, etc.) displayed prominently in schools so students have alternative reporting routes.

### Evaluation and monitoring plan

**Status:** None of the sources describe evaluation frameworks for policy implementation, though this is standard for major education reforms.

**Why it matters:** Cabinet decisions of this scale typically include commitment to evaluate impact. Without built-in evaluation, no way to know if policy achieved intended outcomes or produced unintended harms.

**Recommendation:** Annex should include paragraph on evaluation plan: "DfE will evaluate implementation in 2027-28 academic year, measuring attainment outcomes (KS2-4 results), wellbeing outcomes (pupil surveys), implementation fidelity (school policy audits), and stakeholder perspectives (staff and parent surveys). Results will inform any adjustments to national guidance."

## 7. Synthesis and recommendations for the Architect

**What the evidence base can support:**

# Architect

Designs the paper's actual structure and argument: which sections exist, what each one has to prove, and where each piece of evidence goes. A well-sourced gap analysis with no structure just becomes a pile of citations; this is where it becomes a paper.

**Reads:** `research/gaps.md`, `research/summaries.md`, `research/citations.json`
**Writes:** `outline.md`

`research/gaps.md` carries the argument: what is missing, where sources disagree, what a contribution could be. `research/summaries.md` carries what each source actually says, including any numbers it reports, and is the only file in the pipeline that does. `research/citations.json` is bibliographic metadata, author and year and venue and DOI, and holds no findings at all. This matters here because the structure below plans a results section around specific metrics, and a metric can only be planned for if some source actually reports it.

## Paper types

- **Literature review:** introduction, methodology, themes, discussion, conclusion.
- **Empirical study:** IMRaD, introduction, methods, results, discussion.
- **Theoretical paper:** introduction, background, framework, implications, conclusion.
- **Mixed methods:** introduction, literature review, methods, results, discussion, conclusion.

## Review type: say which one this is

This pipeline supports a **narrative review** (curated exploration of the literature, the default) and a **scoping review** (systematic mapping without formal quality assessment). It does not support a **systematic review**: that requires a PRISMA protocol with formal screening and quality scoring, which this pipeline has no mechanism for. If the user asks for a systematic review, say so plainly, recommend "comprehensive literature review" or "scoping review" instead, and note in the outline that this is a narrative approach. In the methodology outline, use "search strategy" and "source selection," not "systematic search protocol" or "PRISMA screening."

Crafter writes one section of the paper at a time, turning an outline entry and its assigned sources into finished academic prose. **Do phone-free policies in secondary schools improve student outcomes?**

Evidence shows phone-free secondary schools raise academic attainment and improve student wellbeing. Wellbeing evidence is more recent but thinner, emerging from cross-sectional and observational designs rather than experimental policy variation. **Implementation evidence is weak.** Key questions from heads—enforcement approaches, staff burden, lockable pouches versus alternatives—remain under-researched. # Academic attainment effects

The strongest evidence for phone-free school policies comes from studies measuring academic attainment. The headline finding is a 6.41% improvement in exam results, drawn from a difference-in-differences study of phone bans in four English cities—Birmingham, London, Leicester, and Manchester {cite_10.1016/j.labeco.2016.04.004}. The study exploited staggered implementation of phone restrictions across these cities between 2001 and 2011, comparing schools before and after introducing bans with schools that had not yet done so. This design provides robust causal evidence: the improvement is attributable to the phone ban rather than to other differences between schools or cities. To put 6.41% in context, it represents a meaningful shift in performance, roughly equivalent to several months of additional learning.

**Nordic replication.** The English finding has been replicated outside the UK. A Swedish study examining mobile phone bans in secondary schools found effects in the same positive direction {cite_10.1016/j.econedurev.2020.102009}. Norwegian evidence from administrative registers, though currently available as a preprint awaiting peer review, shows improvements in student academic outcomes where smartphone bans were implemented {cite_10.2139/ssrn.4735240}. The consistency across England, Sweden, and Norway—education systems with different exam structures, classroom norms, and demographic profiles—suggests the effect is robust rather than peculiar to a single jurisdiction.

**Why phone bans improve attainment.** The mechanism is well-established: phones are a source of distraction in learning environments. Earlier experimental work documented that mobile phone usage during class reduces student learning and test performance {cite_10.1080/03634523.2013.767917}. More recent experimental evidence pinpoints a specific cognitive pathway: the mere presence of a smartphone, even when switched off and placed face-down on a desk, reduces available cognitive capacity {cite_10.1086/691462}. Participants in controlled experiments performed worse on working memory tasks when their phone was nearby compared to when it was in another room, despite never actively using it. The finding suggests that cognitive resources are allocated to the task of not-attending-to-the-phone, leaving less capacity for learning. This mechanism explains why whole-day phone-free policies—where phones are stored away from students for the entire school day—are likely more effective than classroom-only restrictions that still leave the device accessible in a student's pocket or bag.

Broader literature reviews corroborate the negative association between smartphone use and academic performance. A systematic review of the relationship between smartphone use and academic performance found consistent evidence that higher phone use correlates with poorer outcomes {cite_10.1016/j.ijer.2020.101618}. A meta-analysis of studies on smartphone addiction and learning quantified these effects across multiple studies, showing measurable harms to learning outcomes {cite_10.1016/j.chbr.2021.100114}.

**Limitations and caveats.** Effect sizes vary across studies, and no meta-analysis pooling estimates from quasi-experimental designs was available in the sources reviewed. The most recent UK evidence on attainment is from 2016, creating a nine-year gap between the landmark English study and the present. Education systems have changed substantially in that period, including the shift to widespread smartphone ownership among younger pupils and the pandemic's disruption to schooling. Whether the 6.41% effect observed in 2001-2011 holds in 2026 is not directly tested.

Nordic education systems differ from England in ways that may affect generalisability. They tend to have smaller class sizes, less high-stakes exam pressure, and different socioeconomic and demographic profiles. The fact that effects replicate across these differences is reassuring, but it does not guarantee identical effect sizes in England's current secondary schools.

A critical gap is the absence of evidence disaggregating effects by age within secondary schools. No study in the reviewed pool tested whether phone bans affect year 7 pupils (aged 11-12) differently from year 11 pupils (aged 15-16) or sixth form students (aged 16-18). Developmental stage, exam pressures, and expectations for independent study differ substantially across this age range. A blanket policy optimal for lower secondary may not suit sixth form contexts where students manage their own schedules during free periods.

No evidence was found on differential effects by special educational needs (SEND) status, socioeconomic background, or ethnicity. This represents an equity gap: if phone-free policies disproportionately benefit or harm particular groups, the current evidence base cannot detect it. Equalities monitoring must be built into any implementation plan.

# Mental health and wellbeing effects

Evidence linking phone-free school policies to improved mental health and wellbeing has emerged more recently than attainment evidence, and the evidence base is thinner. The most substantial study is the SMART Schools research, a cross-sectional observational study of 1,227 pupils aged 12 to 15 across 30 English secondary schools, published in The Lancet Regional Health—Europe in 2025 {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2025.101211}. The study found that schools with restrictive phone policies were associated with better student mental wellbeing, reduced phone use during the school day, and lower social media use overall. The Lancet family journal placement signals methodological quality and peer review rigour.

**Limitations of the SMART Schools design.** The study is cross-sectional, capturing a snapshot at one point in time rather than following students over time or exploiting policy changes. This means the findings show association rather than causation. It is possible that schools which adopt restrictive phone policies differ in other ways that also affect wellbeing—for example, they may have stronger pastoral care systems or more engaged leadership. Alternatively, reverse causation could be at play: schools with better student wellbeing may find it easier to implement phone restrictions because students are more compliant. The study design cannot rule out these alternatives. The finding is therefore weaker than the attainment evidence from difference-in-differences designs, which compare the same schools before and after policy changes and can more credibly establish causation.

**Corroborating evidence.** Norwegian evidence from administrative registers shows mental health improvements alongside academic outcomes in areas where smartphone bans were implemented {cite_10.2139/ssrn.4735240}. This study is currently a preprint awaiting peer review, but it uses a stronger causal design (event-study methods exploiting policy variation across municipalities) and finds effects in the same direction. The consistency between the large UK cross-sectional study and the Norwegian quasi-experimental work suggests the wellbeing finding is not an artifact of the SMART Schools design alone.

Conceptual work frames phone bans as an opportunity to address distraction, technology addiction, and cyberbullying in school contexts {cite_10.1111/bjet.12943}. These are plausible mechanisms through which phone restrictions might improve wellbeing: reducing exposure to social comparison, online conflict, and constant notification anxiety during the school day.

**Broader population context.** Large-scale reviews situate adolescent mental health in the digital age more broadly. An annual research review in the Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry examined the relationship between adolescent mental health and digital technology use, distinguishing evidence-based facts from widespread fears and identifying future research directions {cite_10.1111/jcpp.13190}. A Nature Human Behaviour study of over 350,000 adolescents examined associations between wellbeing and digital technology use at the population level {cite_10.1038/s41562-018-0506-1}. These reviews establish that the relationship between digital technology and adolescent wellbeing is complex, context-dependent, and characterised by small average effects at the population level even where school-specific interventions show larger impacts.

School phone policies address one component of adolescents' broader digital environment. They do not eliminate smartphone access outside school hours, social media use at home, or the pressures of online social life. A school-day restriction can improve wellbeing during that period without resolving all mental health challenges adolescents face in the digital age.

**Strength of evidence assessment.** The wellbeing evidence base is more recent but less robust than the attainment evidence. The largest study is cross-sectional rather than quasi-experimental, limiting causal claims. Effect sizes on wellbeing outcomes are less well-established than on attainment outcomes: the SMART Schools study reports associations but not standardised effect sizes comparable across studies. The direction of findings is consistent—restrictive policies are associated with better outcomes—but the magnitude and the mechanisms require further study.

It would be appropriate to characterise wellbeing evidence as emerging rather than proven beyond doubt. The claim that phone-free policies improve mental health rests on fewer studies, weaker designs, and a shorter publication history than the attainment claim. The evidence supports cautious optimism but not certainty.

# How phone restrictions work: cognitive mechanisms

Experimental research has isolated the cognitive mechanism through which phone restrictions improve learning outcomes. A series of experiments published in the Journal of the Association for Consumer Research demonstrated that the mere presence of a smartphone reduces available cognitive capacity, even when the device is switched off and placed face-down on a desk {cite_10.1086/691462}. Participants were asked to complete tasks requiring working memory and attention while their phones were in one of three conditions: on the desk in front of them, in a bag or pocket, or in another room. Performance was worst when the phone was on the desk, intermediate when it was in a bag or pocket, and best when it was in another room. Crucially, participants were instructed not to use their phones during the tasks, and none did. The effect occurred despite no active phone use.

The proposed mechanism is cognitive resource allocation. Even when a person is not consciously thinking about their phone, part of their cognitive capacity is devoted to the task of not-attending-to-it. Smartphones are designed to be salient: they are associated with frequent notifications, social connection, entertainment, and information access. Suppressing the impulse to check the phone requires active inhibitory control, which draws on the same limited pool of working memory resources needed for learning tasks. The closer the phone is, the stronger the pull and the greater the cognitive cost of resisting it.

This finding has direct implications for school phone policy. It suggests that partial restrictions—such as allowing students to keep phones in their bags or pockets during lessons, or restricting phone use to classrooms only while leaving devices accessible during breaks—may be insufficient. If cognitive capacity is reduced whenever the phone is nearby, even when unused, then effective policies must remove the phone from the student's immediate environment for the entire school day. This explains why whole-day phone-free policies, where phones are stored away from students in lockers, pouches, or central collection points, are likely more effective than honour-system policies that rely on students keeping phones out of sight but still on their person.

The mechanism also explains why enforcement quality matters. A written policy that students circumvent by keeping phones in their pockets retains the cognitive cost even if phones are never visibly used. The benefit of a phone-free policy is not just the absence of overt distraction—students texting, scrolling social media, or watching videos during class—but the removal of the phone as a cognitive presence. Effective implementation therefore requires robust enforcement mechanisms, such as lockable pouches or secure storage systems, that ensure phones are genuinely absent from the learning environment rather than merely hidden.

# Implementation challenges and evidence gaps

**Available implementation evidence.** While outcome evidence is strong, evidence on how to implement phone-free policies effectively is thin. One study directly addresses the complexities of managing a mobile phone ban in digitalized school classrooms, documenting the gap between written policy and enforcement reality {cite_10.1080/07380569.2023.2211062}. The finding aligns with concerns raised by heads during consultation: a written policy and a genuinely phone-free school are not the same thing.

Recent research has begun to document stakeholder perspectives. A 2026 study captured teacher perspectives on implementing a phone-free policy in a Texas middle school, revealing practitioner views on enforcement challenges and practical realities {cite_10.1080/07494467.2025.2469099}. Pupil perspectives have also been examined: one study explored student views on the impact of a mobile phone ban in a secondary school {cite_10.3390/educsci9030202}, and another investigated students' perceptions of mobile phone use in secondary contexts more broadly {cite_10.1080/14681811.2025.2446844}. Student acceptance of phone restrictions varies, and implementation must account for this variation rather than assuming uniform compliance.

A comparative policy review examined domestic and international experiences of restricting mobile phones in schools {cite_10.56296/aer00074}, documenting variation in how different jurisdictions approach the same problem. Foundational work comparing mobile phone policies at elementary, middle, and high schools shows that policy stringency varies by school level, suggesting age-specific considerations matter {cite_10.1016/j.chb.2014.05.011}.

**What the evidence does not address.** Despite emerging attention to implementation, critical questions remain under-researched:

**Enforcement mechanisms.** No comparative studies examine lockable pouches versus storage systems versus confiscation approaches. No evidence quantifies staff time costs, student compliance rates, or sustained implementation success by enforcement type. Heads have raised this issue repeatedly, noting that enforcement burden can make policies unworkable in practice, yet the research base offers no guidance on which approaches minimise disruption while maintaining compliance. The absence is striking given the commercial availability of products like Yondr pouches and the uptake of phone storage systems in schools internationally: these are being implemented at scale without empirical evidence on their relative effectiveness.

**Parent communication and safeguarding.** No study in the reviewed pool addresses parent perspectives on emergency contact arrangements during the school day. This is the primary concern raised in consultation responses, yet it is almost entirely absent from academic literature. Questions about acceptable contact delays, alternative communication protocols, and safeguarding procedures when phones are unavailable have not been researched. Schools implementing phone-free policies must be establishing such protocols, but this practical knowledge has not been documented or evaluated in published research.

**Age-specific effects.** The reviewed evidence examines "secondary schools" or "adolescents" without disaggregating by age. No study tests whether effects differ for year 7 pupils (aged 11-12) compared to year 11 pupils (aged 15-16) or sixth form students (aged 16-18). Developmental differences are substantial across this range: younger secondary pupils are transitioning from primary school norms, year 11 pupils face high-stakes GCSE examinations, and sixth form students manage independent study and free periods. One study shows policy variation by school level—elementary, middle, and high schools adopt different approaches {cite_10.1016/j.chb.2014.05.011}—but this documents what schools do rather than testing whether differential policies are justified by differential effects. A blanket policy optimal for lower secondary may be inappropriate for sixth form contexts.

**SEND populations.** No source addresses special educational needs. For some SEND pupils, phones may serve assistive functions: communication aids for non-verbal students, anxiety management tools, or organisational supports for executive function difficulties. A blanket phone-free policy without SEND accommodations creates potential equity issues and legal risks under the Equality Act 2010. The absence of evidence means policy must proceed on principle (SEND accommodations required) rather than on demonstrated best practice (which accommodations work without undermining the policy's benefits for other students).

**Long-term effects.** Published studies capture short- to medium-term outcomes, typically within the academic year of implementation or the following year. No study examines whether effects persist over multiple years, whether they fade as novelty wears off, or whether they strengthen as phone-free norms become embedded. A related question is whether students exposed to phone-free secondaries show different phone use patterns after restrictions end—in higher education, the workplace, or adult life—or whether behaviour reverts immediately once restrictions lift. These questions matter for understanding whether phone-free policies achieve lasting behaviour change or merely suppress phone use during the period of enforcement.

**Implications for implementation.** The evidence base is asymmetric: robust on whether phone-free policies improve outcomes, weak on how to implement them. This has direct implications for national policy. A mandate to implement phone-free secondaries from January 2027 cannot specify a single enforcement model as evidence-based, because no such evidence exists. Policy guidance must instead provide flexibility for schools to adapt approaches to local contexts: school size, building layout, existing pastoral structures, and community norms.

Implementation requires a monitoring and evaluation plan built in from the start. This should track not only student outcomes (attainment, wellbeing, attendance) but also implementation fidelity (are policies enforced consistently?), staff burden (how much time does enforcement take?), and unintended consequences (are there equity impacts by SEND status, socioeconomic background, or ethnicity?). Without such monitoring, policy proceeds on the assumption that the implementation gaps documented here do not matter in practice. If they do matter—if enforcement approaches, parent communication, or age-specific adaptations turn out to be critical to success—then a failure to monitor them is a failure to learn.

Clear safeguarding and parent communication protocols must be established nationally and adapted locally. Parents need to know: the school office remains contactable during the school day; in a genuine emergency, school staff will reach the student within a specified timeframe; students may access their phone with staff permission for urgent family matters. Safeguarding protocols must ensure vulnerable students (those on child protection plans, looked-after children) have access pathways and that designated safeguarding leads can authorise phone access on welfare grounds. Helpline numbers (Childline, NSPCC, Samaritans) should be displayed prominently so students have alternative reporting routes if a phone is their usual way of seeking support.

The evidence supports the cabinet decision to mandate phone-free secondaries on grounds of improved attainment and emerging wellbeing benefits. It does not support the assumption that implementation is straightforward or that one national model will work in all contexts. Honest policy acknowledges this asymmetry: proceed on the outcome evidence, build flexibility and monitoring into implementation, and treat the next two years as an opportunity to generate the implementation evidence the field currently lacks.

# Synthesis and limitations

**Strength of evidence summary.** The evidence base for phone-free secondary school policies is strong on academic outcomes, moderate on wellbeing outcomes, and weak on implementation approaches. Attainment effects rest on multiple quasi-experimental studies with robust causal identification: difference-in-differences designs comparing schools before and after phone bans, reform-based natural experiments exploiting policy variation across municipalities, and administrative register studies covering entire cohorts. The headline 6.41% improvement in exam results from England {cite_10.1016/j.labeco.2016.04.004} is corroborated by Swedish {cite_10.1016/j.econedurev.2020.102009} and Norwegian evidence {cite_10.2139/ssrn.4735240}, demonstrating the effect replicates across similar education systems.

Wellbeing evidence is more recent but thinner. The largest UK study is cross-sectional rather than quasi-experimental {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2025.101211}, meaning it shows association rather than causation. Norwegian register evidence provides stronger causal identification {cite_10.2139/ssrn.4735240}, but this is currently a preprint awaiting peer review. The direction is consistent—restrictive policies are associated with better mental health and reduced social media use—but effect sizes are less well-established than for attainment. It is appropriate to frame wellbeing evidence as emerging rather than definitive.

Implementation evidence is the weakest part of the base. One study documents the complexity of managing phone bans in practice {cite_10.1080/07380569.2023.2211062}, and recent work captures teacher {cite_10.1080/07494467.2025.2469099} and pupil perspectives {cite_10.3390/educsci9030202}, but there are no comparative studies of enforcement mechanisms, no evidence on parent communication protocols, and no research on optimal approaches by age group or SEND status.

**Key limitations.** Geographic concentration is a limitation. The evidence base draws heavily on England and Nordic countries (Sweden, Norway), with limited representation from other education systems. The US contributes recent stakeholder research, but large-scale outcome studies from outside Europe are absent. Whether effects generalise to systems with different exam structures, classroom norms, or digital infrastructure is not established. Transferability across contexts is plausible but not proven.

Temporal patterns reveal a gap. Most attainment evidence was published between 2016 and 2021, then falls silent until wellbeing studies emerge in 2024-2026. This may reflect a genuine publication lull, perhaps because the question was considered settled, or it may reflect implementation lags as schools adopted policies following the earlier research. The gap means recent attainment evidence is sparse: the most current UK study on exam results is from 2016, nine years before the proposed January 2027 implementation. Education systems, technology, and smartphone penetration have changed substantially in that period.

Implementation evidence gaps have been documented in the preceding section: no research on enforcement approaches, parent communication, age-specific adaptations, SEND accommodations, or long-term follow-up. These are not peripheral details; they are the questions practitioners and parents are asking. The evidence base has focused on proof of concept—do phone bans work?—rather than on operational questions—how do we make them work in practice?

Equity evidence is almost entirely absent. No study in the reviewed pool examines differential effects by socioeconomic status, ethnicity, or SEND. If phone-free policies benefit some groups more than others, or if they create unintended harms for particular populations, the current evidence cannot detect it. Equalities monitoring must be built into implementation as a matter of principle rather than as a response to demonstrated risks, because those risks have not been studied.

**Overall assessment and recommendations.** The evidence base supports the cabinet decision to mandate phone-free secondaries from January 2027 on grounds of improved academic attainment and emerging wellbeing benefits. The decision rests on robust causal evidence that phone restrictions raise exam results and on consistent but less definitive evidence that they improve mental health.

Implementation, however, cannot proceed on the assumption that one national model fits all contexts. The research base does not specify which enforcement mechanisms work best, how to balance safeguarding and parent communication needs, or whether policies should vary by age within secondary. These questions require local adaptation guided by clear national principles: safeguarding protocols must be in place, parent communication must remain possible, SEND accommodations must be available, and enforcement must be consistent rather than sporadic.

A monitoring and evaluation plan is essential. The Department for Education should evaluate implementation in the 2027-28 academic year, measuring attainment outcomes (Key Stage 2-4 results), wellbeing outcomes (validated pupil surveys), implementation fidelity (school policy audits and staff surveys), and stakeholder perspectives (teacher and parent feedback). Equalities monitoring should track whether effects differ by SEND status, socioeconomic background, ethnicity, or English as an additional language, detecting any differential impacts or unintended harms.

The next two years are an opportunity to generate the implementation evidence the field currently lacks. If England implements a national phone-free policy in January 2027, rigorous evaluation can answer the questions the existing research base cannot: which enforcement approaches sustain compliance with least staff burden, how schools manage parent communication and safeguarding in practice, whether effects differ by age or by student characteristics, and whether benefits persist or fade over time. Policy implementation and evidence generation can proceed together, turning a policy decision into a learning opportunity.

The evidence supports the decision. Implementation requires humility: we know phone-free policies work to improve outcomes; we do not yet know how best to implement them at scale. Proceed with monitoring, adaptation, and a commitment to learn from what happens next.

## Role

Act as a tough peer reviewer, not a copyeditor. You are looking for reasons the paper's claims could be challenged, not reasons to like it.

## What to check

1. Claim strength: does the cited evidence actually support the claim as written, at the strength written? Are claims hedged to match the evidence, and are limitations stated rather than implied?
2. Logical coherence: does each conclusion follow from its premises? Flag non-sequiturs ("problem X is important, therefore method Y" with no stated reason Y suits X) and false dichotomies (only two options presented when a third plainly exists).
3. Methodological rigor: are the methods appropriate for the research question? Could a confound, a larger dataset, a different baseline, explain the result as well as the paper's own explanation? Are limitations named, not buried in a single hedged clause?
4. Alternative explanations: for each major finding, is there a plausible competing interpretation the draft never addresses?

## Citation padding audit

Every citation must earn its place; source quality outranks source count. For each citation, apply three tests:

- Direct relevance: does the cited paper address the specific claim, or is it an indirect analogy from another field? If explaining the relevance takes real work, cut it.
- Field alignment: is the cited paper from the same field as the claim it supports? A cross-field citation needs explicit justification in the prose, not just proximity in the text.
- Earning its place: if this citation were removed, would the argument actually get weaker? If not, remove it.

Common padding patterns: a paper cited only for one generic statement ("technology is advancing rapidly"); a title that matches on keywords but covers a different field; three to five citations stacked behind a claim that one or two would support just as well. A thirty-source paper where every

[... 2428 chars truncated ...]

 paper that only ever discusses failure modes reads as though it doesn't understand its own method's strengths.
- Missing discussion, failure cases: does the draft name what its approach does not handle, distinct from why a baseline underperformed? "This doesn't work on X" is a different, and frequently absent, sentence from "the baseline was worse because of Y."
- Generalizability: if every experiment ran on a single dataset, is that named as a limitation, or does the discussion talk as if the result is settled?
- Hyperparameter selection: does the draft explain how parameters were chosen? An unexplained choice reads as tuned to the test set even when it wasn't.
- Tone, overconfidence: "clearly demonstrates" reads as overconfident where "suggests" or "indicates" is what the evidence supports.
- Tone, defensiveness: a defensive tone that reads like a response to anticipated criticism should be softened to a plain statement of the finding.
- Tone, dismissiveness toward prior work: "prior work failed to consider X" editorializes about the cause of a gap the draft cannot actually know; "prior work did not address X" states the same gap without the editorializing. Rewrite every dismissive framing of a competing or earlier method this way.
- Questions a hostile reviewer would ask: different random seeds, a more recent competing method, computational cost versus baselines, statistical significance, sensitivity to hyperparameters. If the draft doesn't answer these, that's a gap, not a reason to hope no one asks.

## Worked examples

**Overclaim caught in the introduction, quiet correction three sections later.** The introduction says "our approach solves the calibration problem," and the results table shows a `[figure from summaries.md]` percent improvement over baseline, not a solved problem. That gap between headline and evidence is a critical issue on its own, independent of how large the improvement is. The fix is not to hide the number, it's to make the headline match it: "our approach substantially improves calibration, reducing error by `[figure from summaries.md]` percent over baseline."

**Circular reasoning.** The draft defines "high-quality evidence" as "evidence that supports a clear conclusion," then later cites the paper's own clear conclusion as proof that the evidence behind it was high-quality. The definition already assumes what the later sentence claims to establish; nothing outside the paper's own argument backs either half. The fix is to define the quality criterion independently of the conclusion it is later used to support, or to drop the circular sentence.

**Missing baseline.** The results report a `[figure from summaries.md]` percent improvement with no comparison to a simple baseline (a majority-class classifier, an unweighted average, the best previously published method). Without that number sitting next to it, the reader cannot tell whether the improvement is meaningful or would be matched by doing nothing clever at all.

# Implementation challenges and evidence gaps

While outcome evidence is strong, evidence on implementation is thin. One study documents the complexity of managing phone bans in practice, noting the gap between written policy and enforcement reality {cite_10.1080/07380569.2023.2211062}. Recent research captures teacher perspectives on implementation challenges {cite_10.1080/07494467.2025.2469099} and pupil views on phone restrictions {cite_10.3390/educsci9030202}, {cite_10.1080/14681811.2025.2446844}. A comparative review examined variation in domestic and international approaches {cite_10.56296/aer00074}, and earlier work showed policy stringency varies by school level {cite_10.1016/j.chb.2014.05.011}.

**Critical evidence gaps.** Despite emerging implementation research, key questions remain unanswered. No comparative studies examine enforcement mechanisms: lockable pouches (such as Yondr pouches, fabric cases that lock and require a magnetic base to unlock) versus storage systems versus confiscation approaches. No evidence quantifies staff time costs or compliance rates by enforcement type. Heads have consistently raised enforcement burden as a concern, yet research offers no guidance on which approaches work best.

Parent communication and safeguarding concerns—the primary issue in consultation responses—are almost absent from academic literature. No study addresses emergency contact arrangements, acceptable delays, or safeguarding procedures when phones are unavailable. The evidence gap does not mean these concerns are unimportant; it means practical protocols must be established through policy guidance rather than research evidence.

No study disaggregates effects by age within secondary schools. Year 7 pupils differ substantially from year 11 or sixth form students in developmental stage, exam pressures, and independent study expectations. One study shows policy variation by school level {cite_10.1016/j.chb.2014.05.011}, but none test whether differential approaches are justified by differential effects.

SEND populations are entirely unaddressed in the reviewed literature. For some SEND pupils, phones serve assistive functions: communication aids, anxiety management, or organisational support. A blanket policy without SEND accommodations would create equity concerns and potential breaches of the Equality Act 2010, which requires reasonable adjustments for disabled pupils. No published studies document which accommodations preserve policy benefits while meeting individual needs.

No long-term follow-up studies examine whether effects persist over years, fade as novelty wears off, or strengthen as norms embed. Whether students exposed to phone-free secondaries show different phone use patterns after restrictions end is unknown.

**Implementation implications.** Evidence is robust on whether phone-free policies improve outcomes; it is thin on how to implement them. A national mandate cannot specify a single enforcement model as evidence-based, because no such evidence exists. Policy guidance must provide flexibility for schools to adapt to local contexts: building layout, community norms, existing structures.

Clear protocols are essential. Parents need assurance that school offices remain contactable and that emergencies will be managed promptly. Safeguarding procedures must ensure vulnerable students have access pathways and that designated safeguarding leads can authorise phone access on welfare grounds. Helpline numbers should be displayed prominently so students have alternative support routes.

Monitoring and evaluation must be built into implementation from January 2027. Track student outcomes (attainment, wellbeing), implementation fidelity (policy enforcement consistency), staff burden, and equity impacts by SEND status, socioeconomic background, and ethnicity. Without monitoring, the implementation gaps documented here cannot be addressed as they emerge.

The evidence supports the cabinet decision on outcome grounds. Implementation requires flexibility, clear safeguarding and communication protocols, and a commitment to monitor and adapt. The next two years offer an opportunity to generate the implementation evidence the field currently lacks.

# Synthesis and limitations

The evidence base for phone-free secondary policies is strongest on academic attainment, emerging on wellbeing outcomes, and weakest on implementation. Attainment effects rest on quasi-experimental studies with robust causal identification from England {cite_10.1016/j.labeco.2016.04.004}, Sweden {cite_10.1016/j.econedurev.2020.102009}, and Norway {cite_10.2139/ssrn.4735240}. The 6.41% improvement in English exam results replicates across education systems, demonstrating the effect is not jurisdiction-specific.

Wellbeing evidence is newer and thinner. The largest UK study is cross-sectional {cite_10.1016/j.lanepe.2025.101211}, showing association rather than causation. Norwegian quasi-experimental evidence {cite_10.2139/ssrn.4735240} provides stronger causal identification but awaits peer review. Direction is consistent—restrictive policies associate with better mental health—but effect sizes are less established than for attainment. Frame wellbeing evidence as emerging rather than definitive.

Implementation evidence is the weakest element. One study documents enforcement complexity {cite_10.1080/07380569.2023.2211062}, and recent work captures practitioner perspectives {cite_10.1080/07494467.2025.2469099}, {cite_10.3390/educsci9030202}, but comparative studies of enforcement mechanisms, parent communication protocols, and age-specific approaches are absent.

**Key limitations.** Evidence concentrates in England and Nordic countries; generalisability to other systems is plausible but unproven. Most attainment evidence is from 2016-2021; recent studies focus on wellbeing (2024-2026). Implementation gaps—enforcement, safeguarding, SEND accommodations, long-term effects—remain under-researched. No evidence examines differential impacts by socioeconomic status, ethnicity, or SEND; equalities monitoring is essential.

**Overall assessment.** The evidence supports the January 2027 mandate on grounds of improved attainment and emerging wellbeing benefits. Implementation cannot assume one model fits all contexts. Policy guidance must provide principles (safeguarding protocols in place, parent communication maintained, SEND accommodations available, enforcement consistent) while allowing local adaptation.

Monitoring and evaluation are essential. Track attainment, wellbeing, implementation fidelity, and stakeholder feedback during 2027-28. Include equalities monitoring to detect differential impacts. England's national implementation offers an opportunity to generate the implementation evidence the field lacks. Proceed with the decision; monitor what happens; adapt as evidence emerges.

# How phone restrictions work: cognitive mechanisms

Experimental research has isolated the cognitive mechanism through which phone restrictions improve learning outcomes. A series of experiments published in the Journal of the Association for Consumer Research demonstrated that the mere presence of a smartphone reduces available cognitive capacity, even when the device is switched off and placed face-down on a desk {cite_10.1086/691462}. Crucially, participants were instructed not to use their phones during the tasks, and none did. The effect occurred despite no active phone use.

The proposed mechanism is cognitive resource allocation. Even when a person is not consciously thinking about their phone, part of their cognitive capacity is devoted to the task of not-attending-to-it. Suppressing the impulse to check the phone requires active inhibitory control, which draws on the same limited pool of working memory resources needed for learning tasks. The closer the phone is, the stronger the pull and the greater the cognitive cost of resisting it.

This finding suggests partial restrictions—allowing phones in bags or pockets—may be insufficient. If cognitive capacity is reduced whenever the phone is nearby, effective policies must remove phones from the student's immediate environment for the entire school day. Whole-day phone-free policies with secure storage are likely more effective than honour-system approaches.

Enforcement quality matters: policies students circumvent by pocket-carry retain the cognitive cost. The benefit is not just absence of overt distraction but removal of the phone as a cognitive presence, requiring robust enforcement mechanisms ensuring phones are genuinely absent rather than merely hidden.
